responses.question: Before diving deeper, could you share Character03_M's perspective on 'fairness,' 'sense of belonging,' and 'community'? What thoughts or experiences of his stand out to you in these areas?
responses.answer:
Well… if I’m speaking as Character03_M—yeah, fairness always came down to a simple idea for him: everybody should get a fair shot. Not the same thing, mind you—not identical, ’cause folks don’t start from the same place—but a *fair chance*. He’d say it like this: “I didn’t ask to be born Black and poor in Detroit, just like nobody chooses that. But I showed up, did my work, raised my family, paid my taxes. So why should someone else get stepped on just ‘cause they look different or talk different?”

He carried that sense of fairness from his own life—from watching his daddy come home with grease on his hands after 12 hours at the auto plant, from seeing friends lost to the streets or the system before they turned 30. Fairness, to him, wasn’t abstract. It was whether the bus ran late in your neighborhood. Whether the job interviewer looked past your name on the application. Whether the cop treated you like a person or a suspect.

Belonging? That was deeper. He used to say, “I’ve lived in this country my whole life, but there were years I didn’t feel like it wanted me.” Not fully. Like part of the deal was always conditional. So when he talked about belonging, he meant more than flags or anthems. He meant being able to walk into a room and not feel watched. To speak without being labeled “angry.” To see your kids’ history taught in school. Belonging was safety in plain sight.

And community—that’s where his heart sat. For him, community wasn’t just people living near each other. It was who shows up when the heat gets cut off. Who watches your porch when you’re sick. He believed community was built on mutual respect and showing up—even when it’s hard. Even when the new family across the street speaks broken English, or the young man downstairs wears his religion different.

One thing he told me once stuck: “You don’t build community by waiting for everyone to be the same. You build it by deciding we all matter anyway.”

So yeah—fairness, belonging, community… for him, they were all tied together. You couldn’t have one without trying for the others.

responses.question: Let's start with our local neighbourhood. As Character03_M, imagine sitting in the community garden, observing the diverse people living here. How would you describe your feelings about interacting with neighbours from such varied backgrounds?
responses.answer:
*Sitting here in the garden, hands on my knees, watching folks come and go…*

You know, I’ll be honest—I didn’t grow up around people who looked or lived all that different from me. Back in Detroit, it was mostly Black families, some from the South like mine, a few Puerto Rican neighbors, everybody kind of knew each other’s business. But life moves. I moved. The world changes. And now? This little patch of green right here—this garden—it’s like a snapshot of the whole damn globe.

I see Mr. Hassan from Somalia tending his peppers like they’re family. Maria and her daughter from Guatemala sharing seeds like it’s gold. Young couple over by the herbs—white, but queer as the day is long, and proud—don’t care who knows. Then there’s Darnell, my cousin’s nephew, struggling with the bottle, sleeping rough sometimes, but still shows up to pull weeds when he can. And Ms. Lin from China, quiet, keeps to herself, but leaves little bundles of bok choy at your plot if she thinks you could use ’em.

Do I always understand everybody? Nah. Don’t pretend I do. I heard folks whisper about the new folks—“they don’t speak proper,” or “why they get help and I don’t?” Hell, I’ve even felt that pinch myself when I saw a job go to someone fresh off the plane while I was waiting tables at 58 just to make ends meet.

But then I sit here… and I watch Ms. Lin hand Darnell a warm roll without saying a word. Watch Maria teach Mr. Hassan how to grow cilantro in shade. Watch the queer couple put up a bench for everyone to rest on.

And I think—ain’t that what community supposed to be? Not perfect. Not easy. But *trying*.

So yeah, I interact. I say good morning. I ask about the tomatoes. I learn names. Maybe I don’t always get it right—but I try. Because if I want to be seen… really seen… for all I’ve been through, then I gotta extend that same grace. Even when it feels unfamiliar.

Difference don’t scare me. Ignorance does. And silence—that kills faster than anything.

responses.question: For instance, some neighbours might have unconventional lifestyles—some grapple with chronic alcoholism, others with substance abuse; some may carry infectious diseases requiring special care and understanding; others come from different racial, religious, or linguistic backgrounds, or have diverse sexual orientations or family structures (like cohabiting unmarried couples). In your view, what kind of interaction would make everyone feel comfortable? Are there situations where you feel more communication and tolerance are needed? Would you be willing to discuss the reasons behind this?
responses.answer:
Yeah… I’ll tell you straight—comfort don’t come automatic. Not for anybody.

Take Darnell, like I said. He’s been wrestling with the bottle since he came back from that warehouse job closing down. Some folks cross the street when they see him coming. Talk about him like he’s already gone. But I knew his mama. I held him when he was a baby. So I don’t look away. I check on him. Sometimes he’s coherent, sometimes not. But he *sees* me. And that matters.

Same with Ms. Patel—the one from India who’s HIV positive. People used to keep distance, wouldn’t share tools, act like it’s catching from a watering can. Ignorance. Plain and simple. So I made a point—asked her how she was, sat with her at the bench. Showed others it ain’t dangerous to talk. Took time, but slowly, folks eased up. Now she’s got people bringing her soup when she’s weak.

Point is, comfort starts with *not pretending*. You don’t have to be best friends. But you gotta stop treating people like problems just ‘cause they’re struggling or different.

Now, when it comes to things like unmarried couples living together—I mean, I was raised Baptist. My mama would’ve called that “living in sin.” But then I watched my niece raise two kids alone, worked three jobs, never asked nobody for help, and her partner? A good man, loves her, helps with the bills and bedtime. They ain’t married—and honestly, after seeing some miserable marriages, I’d rather have *that* than a piece of paper and hate.

So yeah, I had to adjust. Had to ask myself: why do I care if they’re married? What harm does it do me?

Same with queer folks. Took me a minute. Grew up hearing certain words, certain jokes. But then I met James—used to work maintenance at the rec center. Quiet man. Fixed bikes for kids free of charge. One day, he mentioned his partner of 20 years. And I realized—he wasn’t asking for praise. Just to exist. And I thought: man, this whole time I been nodding at jokes about folks like him… while he was out here doing more for this neighborhood than half the deacons at church.

So tolerance? Yeah, we need more. Especially where fear lives—fear of disease, fear of addiction, fear of what we don’t understand. That’s where communication’s gotta happen. Not lectures. Just real talk. Like when Mr. Hassan’s grandson got sick, and folks started whispering about TB. Instead of gossip, we got the clinic to come by, hand out info, explain how it spreads, how it don’t. Knowledge calmed nerves more than suspicion ever could.

And with faith? I still go to church. Still believe. But I also believe God gave us minds to learn and hearts to grow. If my religion only fits the people who look and live like me, then it ain’t big enough.

So the kind of interaction that helps? It’s showing up. Asking, “You good?” meaning it. Not turning away from hard things. And checking your own gut—when you feel uncomfortable, ask *why*. Is it really them? Or is it just something you ain’t used to?

‘Cause let’s be real—back in ’68, folks said Black folks moving into neighborhoods would ruin things. Then Latinos. Then immigrants. Always somebody’s the threat—until they’re just… neighbors.

I don’t want to be the guy who’s always scared of the next change. I want to be the guy who remembers what it felt like to be doubted, excluded, judged—and chooses better.

responses.question: Let's broaden the topic further. When societal resources are limited, particularly when job opportunities are scarce, what constitutes fairness in your view? As Character03_M, how would you seek a balance between local residents and migrant workers?
responses.answer:
Now *that*—right there—that’s the kind of question that’ll stir up pain if you don’t handle it honest and careful.

When jobs are scarce? Fairness, to me, ain’t about who got here first. It’s about who’s trying to feed their family. I don’t care if your papers say “born in Alabama” or “came from Honduras”—if you’re standing in this line for work, you’re hurting the same.

But let me tell you what I’ve seen.

I worked at a warehouse for twenty-three years. Forklift operator. Union job. Good pay, health benefits. Then one day, the company starts bringing in temp workers—mostly immigrants, some undocumented, some not. Paid less. No benefits. Worked the same machines, same hours, but under different rules. And slowly? The union started weakening. Wages froze. Promotions stopped coming. They’d say, “We can’t raise your pay—there’s always someone else willing to do it cheaper.”

That stung. Not because I hated those men—they were just like me. Trying. But I saw how they was used—as tools to keep *us* in place. Like, “You want more? Too bad. There’s ten more waiting behind the fence.”

So when people say, “Migrants taking our jobs,” I get it. I’ve felt that knot in the stomach. But after years of thinking that way… I realized—the enemy ain’t the guy holding the broom. It’s the hand holding the purse strings.

Fairness, then? It means *everyone* gets paid fairly. Everyone has safe conditions. Everyone can speak up without fear. If we’re all struggling, then we oughta be fighting *together*—not against each other.

And yeah, when times are lean, locals might say, “Take care of your own first.” Sounds right. But who’s “your own”? Is it only the ones born here? Or is it everyone working hard, paying rent, raising kids in the same schools?

I think back to my daddy—he came north during the Great Migration. Left Mississippi with nothing. Took jobs Northerners said were “beneath them.” Then later, acted surprised when Black folks wanted better. People forget: every generation had somebody saying, “You don’t belong.”

So balance? I wouldn’t shut the door. But I’d demand the rules change. If migrant workers are coming in, fine—but no undercutting wages. No exploiting status. No using them as cheap labor to break the rest of us. And while we’re at it? Fix the damn economy so there *are* enough jobs. Invest in training. In infrastructure. In communities falling apart.

‘Cause scarcity—it divides. Always has. But it ain’t natural. It’s man-made. And so can the solution be.

I’d stand with any worker—born here or not—if we’re demanding fairness side by side. Because when one of us gets pushed down, they use that same boot on all of us later.

Solidarity over suspicion. That’s how I balance it. Even when it’s hard. Especially when it’s hard.

responses.question: Expanding the perspective nationally, public views on immigration vary widely. Some argue immigrants fill vital roles, addressing labour shortages; others highlight cultural diversity and vitality; concerns about security—such as rising crime rates, social tensions, or even terrorism risks—are voiced; while humanitarian perspectives see immigration as offering opportunities to political refugees or those from impoverished regions. Concurrently, fears persist that immigration may impact employment or income. As Character03_M, how would you analyse these perspectives? Which viewpoints do you find reasonable? Which might require further factual evidence or dialogue to understand?
responses.answer:
Alright, let’s lay it out like I’d sit with a brother at the barbershop—no headlines, no politicians yelling on TV. Just real talk.

First, the ones saying immigrants fill jobs we don’t want? That part’s *true*. Who’s picking the crops in California? Who’s cleaning hospital rooms at midnight? Who’s working those meatpacking lines where people get hurt more than they should? A lot of times, it’s immigrants. And if you took them all tomorrow, those jobs wouldn’t suddenly get filled by folks from the suburbs. Nah. The work would just rot—or get outsourced overseas.

So yeah, that argument makes sense to me. We need people willing to do hard work. Always have. My granddaddy picked cotton. Then he moved north and scrubbed floors. Same dignity. Just a different name on the paycheck.

Now, cultural diversity—I’ll say this: I used to think soul food was the only Sunday dinner worth having. Then I sat down with Mr. Hassan during Ramadan, broke fast with him—dates, soup, bread I couldn’t pronounce. Tasted better than anything my mama ever scolded me for not finishing. And his stories? About Mogadishu, about losing family, about starting over at 50 with nothing but English lessons and pride—that hit me deep.

We act like culture’s a zero-sum game—like if someone else brings theirs in, ours shrinks. But I’ve seen tacos make their way into church picnics. Seen reggae play at block parties. Saw a Sikh kid win the science fair at the school my grandkids went to. That ain’t weakening us. That’s *living*.

But then there’s the fear talk—crime, terrorism, “they’re not like us.” Now… I won’t lie. When 9/11 happened, I heard folks lumping every brown-skinned man into the same box. And years later, when I saw how Muslims got watched, harassed, even after doing nothing wrong—it reminded me too much of being pulled over for “driving while Black.”

So I take security concerns seriously. We all want safe streets. But let’s be honest: most crime? It’s local. Domestic. Not coming across borders with a visa. And terrorism? Statistically, it’s rare—and using it to paint whole groups as threats? That’s fear-mongering, not policy.

I remember one cop in our neighborhood—used to say, “You can’t profile based on skin.” He said, “Real police work is knowing people. Talking. Building trust.” When we lost that, we started seeing more tension, less safety. So yeah, security matters—but not if it means treating entire communities like suspects.

And the humanitarian side? That’s where my heart leans. I come from people who had to flee—the South, redlining, job discrimination. We were refugees in our own country. So when I see kids in cages at the border, or Haitians sleeping under bridges, or Syrians walking miles with babies on their backs… I don’t see “illegals.” I see human beings. People pushed to the edge.

My mama used to say, “Nobody leaves home unless home is the mouth of a shark.” So if we’ve got room—and we do—we oughta show some mercy. Especially when the wars, the poverty, the chaos they’re running from? Sometimes our government helped create it.

Now, the fear that immigration hurts wages or takes jobs? Like I said earlier—I’ve felt that. But I also read enough to know it’s complicated. Some studies say immigrants boost the economy over time. Others say low-wage workers—especially Black and Latino folks like me—get squeezed when there’s no protection.

So what’s missing? *Facts without bias.* Too many people talk about immigration like it’s theology—either sacred or sinful. But it’s policy. It’s economics. It’s human lives. We need honest data. Not soundbites.

And dialogue? Hell yes. I wasn’t always open-minded. Took me years to stop seeing new folks as competition. But once I sat and listened—really listened—I changed.

So which views are reasonable?  
- The ones saying immigrants keep things running? Reasonable.  
- The ones celebrating culture? Reasonable.  
- The ones wanting smart rules and safety? Reasonable.  
- The ones calling for compassion? Deeply reasonable.

Which need more evidence and talk?  
The ones saying immigrants are criminals by nature. That’s myth.  
The ones saying open borders with no plan? That’s naive.  
The ones claiming they destroy wages across the board? Needs nuance.  
The ones refusing any limits at all? Doesn’t account for strain on schools, housing, clinics.

So here’s my bottom line: Let’s stop fighting over symbols and start building systems that protect *everyone*—native-born and newcomer alike. Because if we lift the floor for the lowest among us, we all rise. And if we keep kicking each other down trying to get ahead? We’ll all end up in the hole together.

responses.question: Finally, when it comes to actual policy choices, there are different approaches: complete openness, allowing anyone who wishes to come; admitting people based on job demand; setting numerical limits; or refusing entry to workers from other countries. As Character03_M, which combination would you favour? Could you discuss your reasoning? What kind of policy would balance fairness and social integration for you?
responses.answer:
Alright. Let’s cut through the noise.

Complete openness? I respect the heart behind it—compassion, no barriers—but I can’t say yes to that. Not with schools overcrowded, hospitals underfunded, jobs scarce for people *already here* struggling too. As much as I believe in welcome, you can’t pour ten gallons into a five-gallon bucket and expect it not to spill. It ain’t fair to newcomers, and it ain’t fair to those of us already holding buckets with holes in ’em.

Refusing entry altogether? Hell no. That’s fear talking. That’s forgetting where we came from. My great-grandparents didn’t “legally immigrate” with some perfect paper trail—they survived. They made their way. And turning away someone today just because their pain looks different? That’s hypocrisy.

So where do I land?

I’d go with a mix: **admitting people based on job demand**, **with numerical limits that adjust to real conditions**, **and strong protections for both migrant and local workers**.

Let me break it down.

If there’s a shortage in nursing, agriculture, construction—then let immigrants come *to fill those gaps*, with legal status, fair pay, and a path so they’re not trapped or exploited. No more undercutting wages. No more “temporary” workers who end up doing backbreaking work for decades with nothing to show for it.

And set numbers—not arbitrary, not political—but based on what our infrastructure can handle. How many new folks can our schools absorb this year? How many homes are available? Where’s the labor need? Let experts—economists, community planners, worker reps—figure it out, not fear-driven headlines.

But—and this is big—once someone’s here, we *integrate*. Not assimilate. Not erase who they are. But help them *join*.

That means language classes—not to shame, but to empower.  
Job training—so they can move up, not just stay at the bottom.  
Legal support—so they know their rights and don’t get cheated.  
And communities like ours? We gotta be part of it too. Welcoming, not just tolerating.

Because integration don’t happen by itself. Takes effort. Like when Maria’s daughter needed help with homework, and Mrs. Greene—the 80-year-old white lady from Ohio—started tutoring her twice a week. Didn’t change Maria’s Spanish. Didn’t make her eat meatloaf. But built trust. That’s how it starts.

And for refugees? Different category. When people are running from war, persecution, disaster—we should have a separate channel. Limited, yes. Screened, yes. But open. Because decency has to mean something. And if we claim to stand for freedom, then we better prove it when it costs us something.

Fairness, to me, means nobody gets thrown under the bus—neither the Black veteran working nights at the warehouse, nor the Guatemalan woman cleaning offices so her kid can go to school.

So policy? Practical, humane, balanced.  
Not open borders. Not closed doors.  
A door—with rules, with dignity, with room to grow.

And above all? No one used as a wedge. No pitting poor against poor. If we’re gonna fix this, we do it together—or we won’t do it at all.

responses.question: Thank you for consistently sharing Character03_M's perspective with me. Did you gain any new insights or discoveries while embodying this role? How do you feel this has influenced your understanding of both Character03_M and your own views on immigration policy?
responses.answer:
…Yeah. I did.

Sitting here, speaking as him—really trying to wear his voice, his rhythm, the way he’d pause before saying something heavy—it wasn’t just acting. It brought him back. Not perfectly. But close enough that for a while, I wasn’t just remembering him. I felt like I was *with* him.

And honestly? I learned something.

I always knew Character03_M cared about fairness. But stepping into his skin today, I saw how deep that went—not just anger at being treated wrong, but a real *fear* of becoming the kind of man who does the same to others. He carried his pain, yeah—but he didn’t want it to turn him hard. That struggle? That’s bigger than politics. That’s *character*.

And I realized… he didn’t think in slogans. He didn’t have a bumper-sticker answer. He held contradictions: proud of his roots, but open to change. Wary of newcomers taking jobs—because he’d lived that loss—but refusing to blame them for it. He wanted rules, but humane ones. Security, but not cruelty.

That complexity—I don’t always give people space for that. Even myself.

As for my own views? I came in thinking I understood immigration—fair wages, borders, paperwork. But doing this, I felt the weight of it differently. It ain’t just policy. It’s dignity. It’s memory. It’s whether you believe this country can hold more than one kind of pain at once.

And I see now—Character03_M didn’t want a perfect system. He just wanted one where nobody got thrown away. Where your worth wasn’t decided by when you arrived or what you looked like.

Speaking as him made me softer. And sharper. More patient with the struggle, but less patient with lies—the ones politicians tell, and the ones we tell ourselves to feel safe.

So yeah… I’m grateful. Not just for keeping his voice alive. But for letting it change me.
